name: MathlibAnnex.WeakDivergenceZero.exists_eqOn
title: A continuous function with zero weak gradient is constant

content.display_title: A continuous function with zero weak gradient is constant
content.one_sentence_role: Removes the exceptional set using continuity and positivity of open sets.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional real normed vector space with its Borel structure and an additive Haar measure $\mu$. Let $U\subseteq E$ be open and preconnected. Let $u:E\to\mathbb R$ be locally integrable and continuous on $U$, and suppose
$$\int_Uu(z)\operatorname{div}W(z)\,d\mu(z)=0$$
for every $C^1$ vector field $W:E\to E$ for which a compact set $K_W$ satisfies
$$\overline{\{z\in E:W(z)\ne0\}}\subseteq K_W\subseteq U.$$
Here $\operatorname{div}W(z):=\operatorname{tr}(DW(z))$. Then there is $c\in\mathbb R$ such that
$$u(x)=c\qquad\text{for every }x\in U.$$
content.assumptions: Preconnectedness means that $U$ has no partition into two disjoint nonempty relatively open subsets; the empty set is allowed. In addition to openness, this condition, local integrability on $U$, and the weak equation, continuity is required only on $U$. The ambient space may have dimension zero. No global regularity, boundedness, or normalization of Haar measure is required.
content.conclusion: The same constant obtained by the almost-everywhere theorem works pointwise on $U$. There is no assertion about values outside $U$.
content.proof_summary: First obtain a common constant almost everywhere. If a point had a different value, continuity would create a nonempty open neighborhood of different values, contradicting almost-everywhere equality.

proof_steps.text:
**Fix the almost-everywhere constant.** Apply [the global almost-everywhere constancy theorem](https://github.com/r-tanaka-math/mathlib-annex/blob/437e6e46228bbb8e91211ebded349d7a30020e73/MathlibAnnex/Analysis/Distribution/WeakGradient.lean#L21-L28) to openness, preconnectedness, local integrability, and the weak equation. It gives a real $c$ with
$$u=c\qquad\mu|_U\text{-almost everywhere}.$$
This step does not use continuity.

**Exclude any exceptional point.** The [open-set continuity lemma](https://github.com/leanprover-community/mathlib4/blob/360da6fa66c1273b76b6b2d8c5666fd5ac2e3b56/Mathlib/MeasureTheory/Measure/OpenPos.lean#L113-L127) applies to $u$ and the constant function with this same $c$: both are continuous on the open set $U$, they agree almost everywhere there, and every nonempty open set has positive measure. Its contradiction argument is as follows. Suppose $x\in U$ and $u(x)\ne c$. Set $\delta=|u(x)-c|/2>0$. Continuity on the open set $U$ provides an open neighborhood $V$ of $x$, contained in $U$, such that $|u(y)-u(x)|<\delta$ for all $y\in V$. Then
$$|u(y)-c|\geq |u(x)-c|-|u(y)-u(x)|>\delta\qquad(y\in V).$$
The almost-everywhere equality restricted to $V$ says $u=c$ there almost everywhere. But $V$ is nonempty and open, so $\mu(V)>0$ and it contains a point satisfying that equality, a contradiction. Thus no such $x$ exists and $u=c$ on $U$. If $U$ is empty, the pointwise conclusion is vacuous.

content.lean_realization_notes: Pointwise equality and almost-everywhere equality are different conclusions. The upgrade here uses both continuity and the positive measure of every nonempty open subset; the weak equation alone does not justify changing values on an exceptional set into pointwise information.
